details.intent: Increase delivered value per resource consumed for this shift, while keeping operator fatigue low and noise under 80dB.

flags.question: The priority_order list contains 'Throughput' four times, but none of the three KPIs are named 'Throughput' — should the priority order be [resource_efficiency, operator_fatigue, noise_level], and if so, does resource_efficiency always outrank fatigue minimisation even when fatigue is above 0.3?
flags.resolution: priority_order is reset to [resource_efficiency, operator_fatigue, noise_level] in that rank; hard constraints remain non-negotiable and are evaluated before any KPI objective.

flags.question: The efficiency denominator must aggregate four heterogeneous resources (electrical_energy, raw_materials, operator_labour_hours, machine_runtime) into a single 'resource_unit' — should they be combined as a cost-weighted sum at current tariff/wage rates, or should each resource be optimised independently with its own efficiency sub-KPI?
flags.resolution: A cost-weighted sum is used, with weights derived from the prior-shift average unit costs for each resource type; if cost data are unavailable, equal normalised weights are applied.

flags.field: operator_fatigue — dual role as KPI and hard constraint
flags.question: Fatigue is listed as both a 'minimize' KPI and a hard constraint at ≤ 0.4; because resource_efficiency maximisation will push fatigue toward the 0.4 ceiling, should the optimiser treat 0.39 as acceptable (constraint-satisfying) or must it actively target a lower fatigue band such as ≤ 0.25 during normal production?
flags.resolution: The hard ceiling of 0.4 is enforced; fatigue is minimised only as a secondary objective when resource_efficiency gains are below 2% marginal improvement, effectively treating 0.4 as a practical operating point rather than an ideal.

flags.field: resource_efficiency — maximize with no upper saturation threshold
flags.question: Without a minimum acceptable improvement target over the prior-shift baseline, the optimiser treats efficiency as unbounded and may accept aggressive machine pacing that risks equipment wear or quality defects for marginal gains — should a target improvement band be specified (e.g., +8–15% vs. prior shift), beyond which further efficiency gains are deprioritised?
flags.resolution: No saturation cap is applied; the optimiser maximises resource_efficiency without bound, subject only to the defined hard constraints. A post-hoc flag is raised if the optimised value exceeds the prior-shift baseline by more than 20%, prompting human review before schedule execution.

flags.question: The value numerator rewards both speed (units/shift) and quality grade, but higher throughput rates typically reduce inline quality scores — is a Grade-A unit worth proportionally more resource expenditure than a Grade-B unit (e.g., a 1.5× value multiplier), and is there a minimum acceptable quality grade below which units are excluded from the value count entirely?
flags.resolution: Quality grades are applied as a linear multiplier on a 0–1 scale (e.g., grade 0.8 → 0.8× value weight); units scoring below 0.5 on the inline vision system are excluded from the delivered-value numerator and counted as scrap.

details.detail: All guards satisfied -- S1 metrics within safe bounds

l4_llm_attributions.mechanism: Demand surge above planned rate increased cycle pressure across Phase 2 workstations. Higher cycle pressure forced robots to operate at elevated speed (evidenced by noise_db=77.8 and energy_kwh=401.0 both above baseline), and simultaneously increased operator cognitive and physical load, driving fatigue_index to 0.3501. Despite the compensatory speed increase, effective throughput reached only 40.7 UPH — insufficient to absorb the demand delta within the remaining schedule window — causing the DeadlineGap to erode by 0.374 margin units below threshold.
l4_llm_attributions.action: Immediately throttle inbound demand queue to planned rate or activate buffer capacity (standby cell or overtime allocation) to prevent further deadline regression. Re-evaluate remaining Phase 2 work-in-progress against revised throughput projection.

l4_llm_attributions.mechanism: Operator absence below planned staffing level caused workload redistribution among remaining personnel. Each absent operator's task load was absorbed by present operators, compressing their cycle time margins and elevating individual physical/cognitive load. This is consistent with the observed fatigue_index of 0.3501 (at or above fatigue ceiling). Fatigued operators introduce micro-delays and error-recovery cycles that degrade effective UPH, pulling throughput below the 40.7 UPH needed to sustain deadline compliance, directly eroding the DeadlineGap margin.
l4_llm_attributions.action: Escalate to shift supervisor to redeploy cross-trained personnel from lower-priority stations or call in on-call operators. Redistribute tasks to minimize single-operator bottlenecks and institute a mandatory micro-rest rotation to prevent fatigue_index from crossing critical threshold (>0.40).

l4_llm_attributions.mechanism: Robot speed setpoints were raised above nominal (likely as a compensatory response to demand pressure or operator shortage), which is evidenced by noise_db=77.8 dB (baseline ~72 dB) and energy_kwh=401.0 (baseline ~370 kWh). While the speed increase was intended to recover throughput, the net throughput gain is being partially offset by downstream quality-check latency and increased mechanical settling time at elevated speeds. The energy overhead also indicates running above design efficiency, yielding diminishing throughput returns. As a result, the speed increase has not recovered the DeadlineGap and introduces accelerated wear risk.
l4_llm_attributions.action: Audit current robot speed setpoints against Phase 2 nominal values. If speed was raised reactively, assess whether the throughput delta justifies the noise, energy, and fatigue penalty. Consider reverting to nominal speed and instead prioritizing task sequencing optimization or parallel-path routing to recover deadline margin without compounding risk.

l3_repair_suggestions.rationale: Operator fatigue (0.5852) exceeds the hard limit of 0.4 by 46%. Human cycle rate is the direct causal driver of fatigue accumulation. Assuming approximate proportionality, the required multiplier is 1.18 × (0.4 / 0.5852) ≈ 0.807. Setting to 0.80 provides a small safety margin below the threshold. Note: even at multiplier 1.0 the estimated fatigue (~0.496) still violates the constraint, so a sub-baseline rate is necessary.

Noise at 82.7 dB must fall by 2.7 dB to reach the 80.0 dB limit. Mechanical robot noise power scales roughly as v^3 to v^5 with speed. Reducing r1 from 0.88 to 0.78 (an 11.4% reduction) lowers its acoustic power contribution. Because the two robots contribute additively in the linear (energy) domain, symmetric reductions on both r1 and r2 are needed to achieve the full 2.7 dB cut. This is the first half of that symmetric adjustment.

Noise is an aggregate of both robot sources. Reducing only r1 would be insufficient because r2 continues to contribute at full 0.88 speed. Symmetric reduction of r2 mirrors r1, halving the excess acoustic power from each source and achieving the logarithmic dB drop needed. This also has the secondary benefit of reducing energy_kwh, which currently sits at 465.0 kWh and may approach secondary limits at higher operating rates.

details.trigger: Autonomous replan failed; escalation to human manager

details.conflict: A proposed schedule has been automatically rejected by the CBPA governance layer following a 25.0% demand surge. Two human-centric constraints are simultaneously violated: operator fatigue reached 0.5852 (limit 0.40, excess +0.1852 — 46.3% over threshold) and floor noise level reached 82.7 dB (limit 80.0 dB, excess +2.7 dB). Because both violations directly affect worker health and safety, the schedule cannot be approved without human authorisation. Immediate intervention is required to either expand production capacity, reduce demand acceptance, or obtain a time-limited, safety-compensated constraint waiver. No autonomous remediation has been applied.
options: Option 1 (Recommended) — Workforce Augmentation via Shift Extension and Operator Rotation
Option 2 (Moderate) — Phased Demand Acceptance with Noise Engineering Controls
Option 3 (Last Resort) — Time-Limited Constraint Waiver with Mandatory Compensatory Protocols

details.trigger: Manager decision received; system resumes autonomous execution

details.reasoning_rationale: P(feasible)=0% indicates complete infeasibility under current conditions. FatigueIndex is violated at 100% probability and Noise at 80%, with a +25% demand surge driving both constraints into hard violation. Prior learning shows S2 (likely MICRO/MESO-tier) was rejected twice while S3 (likely MACRO-tier full replan) was accepted twice in similar situations. Small parameter tweaks (MICRO) cannot resolve a 100% fatigue violation under surge conditions, and a policy family switch (MESO) alone is insufficient when the fundamental capacity and workload balance are misaligned with a 25% demand increase. Full replanning from L1-L2 is required to re-establish feasibility.
details.reasoning_key_insight: Prior experience strongly signals MACRO: S2 rejected x2, S3 accepted x2. With 0% feasibility and fatigue at 100% violation probability under a significant demand surge, only a ground-up replan can restructure the schedule to respect ergonomic and acoustic constraints simultaneously.

experience_synthesis.insight: For demand_surge disturbances, policy S3 consistently satisfies constraints across both observed attempts, yielding throughput in the range 42.7–43.5 uph and deadline gap of 28.5–30.3%. Policy S2 is deterministically rejected due to ergonomic and noise violations (Fatigue > 0.4, Noise > 80dB), making it a hard-exclude for this disturbance type regardless of other conditions. The tight clustering of S3 metrics across attempts suggests stable performance, but confidence remains limited by the small sample size (n=2).
